| App Kit Earn | Anyone. USDC and EURC on Arc. | Non-custodial vault shares over lending protocols (Morpho named). Performance fee 0–50% and management fee 0–5%/yr come from returns. No same-chain deposit fee. Withdrawal fee 0 (subject to change). Principal can drop in extreme markets. Use exploreVaults({ chain, sortBy: "apy" }), getDepositQuote, deposit, getPosition, withdraw. |
| USYC | Allowlisted, non-US institutions, $100k minimum on mainnet | Tokenized T-bill money market fund. Mint and redeem vs USDC through the Teller. Hackathon slides pitch it as "the reserve that earns while it waits". Testnet access needs a support ticket, so plan ahead. |
| Launch DeFi (Aave, Morpho, Uniswap per press) | Permissionless | Not documented in Arc docs. Check each protocol for Arc addresses. |

entries.title: Stablecoins, FX, and yield on Arc: Treasury-agent pattern (how the pieces fit)
entries.text:
1. See: Unified Balance getBalances (crosschain USDC) plus eth_getBalance and balanceOf on Arc, and EURC balanceOf.
2. Forecast and decide: offchain LLM logic with oracle prices.
3. Move: kit.unifiedBalance.spend or kit.bridge to bring USDC onto Arc; kit.swap USDC→EURC for EUR payables.
4. Pay: Memo-wrapped transfers for reconciliation, or Multicall3From for batch payroll.
5. Park: kit.earn.deposit or USYC for surplus. Withdraw ahead of forecast payables.
6. Prove: log every tx hash, memoId, and App Kit traceId. Optionally record an ERC-8004 reputation or ERC-8183 job.

entries.title: Memos, batching, and indexing USDC on Arc: Memo: invoice or order reference on a payment
entries.text:
Contract (mainnet and testnet): 0x5294E9927c3306DcBaDb03fe70b92e01cCede505

- The Memo contract forwards data to target through the CallFrom precompile, so USDC sees your EOA as msg.sender, not the Memo contract.
- Log order: BeforeMemo(i), then the target's events (e.g. USDC Transfer), then Memo(...). Nested memos are supported.
- If the child reverts, the whole tx reverts with MemoFailed(bytes).
- EOA only. Calls from ERC-4337 smart accounts, Circle modular wallets, Circle SCA wallets, or Safe revert because sender spoofing is not allowed. A STATICCALL or DELEGATECALL into Memo also fails. Calling CallFrom directly from an EOA reverts with unauthorized caller. For SCA-based agents, either sign a separate EOA memo tx or keep the metadata offchain.
- Memo data is public. Don't put PII or confidential invoice contents in it. Use a hash or opaque ID.

entries.title: Memos, batching, and indexing USDC on Arc: Multicall3From: atomic batch payouts that keep the sender
entries.text:
Contract (both networks): 0x522fAf9A91c41c443c66765030741e4AaCe147D0

- Each subcall runs with msg.sender = the calling EOA, so USDC.transfer debits your wallet directly with no approval to a batcher.
- Constraints: EOA only. There is no aggregate3Value, because CallFrom doesn't forward native value, so pay through the ERC-20 interface. It emits no batch event; verify one USDC Transfer per subcall with from = your wallet.
- Use allowFailure: false for all-or-nothing payroll. Simulate first (simulateContract).

You can nest: a Multicall3From subcall can target Memo, which lets one batch carry a memo per payee. The docs don't show this, so test it on testnet first.

Compliance note: offchain blocklist and screening systems must account for Memo and Multicall3From routing, because the original caller appears as the sender in subcalls (contract-addresses warning, compliance how-to).

entries.title: Memos, batching, and indexing USDC on Arc: Standard Multicall3 (reads)
entries.text: 0xcA11bde05977b3631167028862bE2a173976CA11. viem's multicall uses it automatically (it's in the chain definition).

entries.title: Memos, batching, and indexing USDC on Arc: EIP-3009 gasless USDC (user signs, relayer pays gas)
entries.text:
USDC EIP-712 domain on Arc testnet: { name: "USDC", version: "2", chainId: 5042002, verifyingContract: "0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000" } (mainnet: same, but chainId: 5042). name() returns "USDC" and version() returns "2" on both networks (eth_call, 2026-09-29). Note that the name is "USDC", not "USD Coin" as on Ethereum.

This is the basis of x402 "exact" payments. receiveWithAuthorization also exists on FiatToken. A blocklisted from or to reverts and burns the relayer's gas.

entries.title: Memos, batching, and indexing USDC on Arc: Detecting incoming USDC (AR agents, deposit watchers)
entries.text:
Two emitters, same topic0 = 0xddf252ad1be2c89b69c2b068fc378daa952ba7f163c4a11628f55a4df523b3ef:

| Emitter | Decimals | Fires on |
|---|---|---|
| 0xffffFFFfFFffffffffffffffFfFFFfffFFFfFFfE (system, EIP-7708) | 18 | Every USDC movement: native sends, the ERC-20 transfer's native leg, mint/burn (from/to = 0x0), CREATE endowments, SELFDESTRUCT |
| 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 (ERC-20) | 6 | ERC-20 interface calls only |

Rules: to catch all incoming USDC, filter the system emitter. Filtering 0x3600… misses plain native sends. Never sum both streams, since one ERC-20 transfer logs twice. The system log comes first in the tx. There is no log for zero-value transfers, self-transfers, or gas. Credit after 1 confirmation (final).

EURC, cirBTC, and other ERC-20s still use their own contract Transfer events.
To backfill testnet history from before Zero5, read NativeCoinTransferred, NativeCoinMinted, and NativeCoinBurned from 0x1800…0000 (usdc-system-events).
Alternatives: Circle Contracts event monitors and webhooks (monitor-contract-events), and the indexers in ecosystem-and-infrastructure.md (Alchemy webhooks, Goldsky, Envio, The Graph, Zerion subscriptions).

entries.title: Architecture: One brain
entries.text:
agentTurn() in packages/agent serves chat and voice alike: the voice worker sends what it heard to the same turn,
with the same tools, limits and thread. The model (OpenAI gpt-5.6-luna by default, chosen through a model registry) only
proposes: no tool takes a network, an address or an "approve" flag. Code resolves the recipient, runs the policy, builds
the transaction and executes it.

entries.title: Architecture: Pure policy, explicit intents
entries.text:
- packages/policy is a pure function from facts to results (errors, refusals, preconditions, clarifications, warnings)
  plus the route: the allowance or a wallet signature. It runs when a card is drafted, again on approval with fresh
  facts, and again at execution.
- packages/intents defines each action as a versioned, EIP-712-hashed draft (SendDraft, SwapDraft, BridgeDraft,
  EarnDraft). An approval names the exact version it approves; a change makes a new version.
- Resolve and resume: when something is missing (a contact, a currency, a sign-in), the fix continues the same intent
  instead of starting over.

entries.title: Architecture: Money paths
entries.text:
- Allowance sends: a spend-ledger reservation under a per-user lock, then Kawase's agent wallet (a Circle
  developer-controlled wallet) redeems your delegation; the receipt's Transfer log is compared with the draft.
- Wallet-signed actions (above the allowance, swaps, bridges, earn): the api builds the exact transaction — for App
  Kit operations, the kit's calls are captured and checked, then wrapped into one EIP-7702 self-batch — the device signs
  it with Face ID, and the api verifies the signed bytes against the draft before broadcasting.
- Bridges are tracked in three legs: the burn on Arc, Circle's attestation, and the mint on the destination chain.
- Automations run in the api's runner every 30 seconds: each occurrence is claimed exactly once, re-checked on fresh
  facts and paid through the same send, earn or bridge path under the automation's own grant.
- Idempotency everywhere: a Circle idempotency key is stored before calling Circle; raw transactions store their hash
  before broadcast; ambiguous outcomes become unknown_outcome and are only re-checked, never re-sent.

entries.title: Architecture: Data
entries.text:
Postgres 17 with Drizzle is the only store and the only message bus: an outbox written in the same transaction as each
change, pg_notify to fan events out over server-sent events, and an inbox table as the source of truth for
notifications. Money is stored as exact base units (numeric(78,0), bigint in TypeScript); ids are UUIDv7.

entries.title: What works today
entries.text:
This page is generated from the code. Kawase keeps one capability registry (packages/config/src/capabilities.ts): the
app reads it to decide what to offer, and the agent reads it before it proposes anything. The docs import the same
registry when the site is built, so they cannot promise more than the app does.

- Available: shipped and offered on that network.
- Coming: part of the product plan, not shipped yet. Areas of the plan that the registry does not list yet are shown
  as coming as well.
- Not on this network: by design (for example, test money exists only on testnet).

entries.title: What works today: What each capability covers
entries.text:
A capability being available doesn't mean every variation of it works. The registry also says, precisely, what runs today
and what doesn't yet — the agent uses the same text to answer "can you…?" honestly.

entries.title: FAQ: Is Kawase a bank or a custodian?
entries.text:
No. Your money sits in your own account on Arc. Kawase holds permissions you signed — a daily allowance and one grant
per automation — and the chain enforces their limits. See the safety model.

entries.title: FAQ: Do I need crypto experience?
entries.text:
No. You talk to Kawase like you would to a person: "send 20 dollars to Alex". There are no seed phrases, gas settings or
PINs. Sign in with an email code, Apple or Google.

entries.title: FAQ: Does the AI decide where my money goes?
entries.text:
It proposes; code decides and the chain enforces. The model cannot choose the network, invent an address or approve a
payment. Inside your allowance it sends to people you've paid before or named; anything else waits for your Face ID.

entries.title: FAQ: What if the AI misunderstands me?
entries.text:
Every action is shown as a card with the exact amount, currency, recipient and network before anything moves, and what was
heard by voice is always shown in words. A newer request in the same conversation cancels an older open card, so an old card
can't be approved by mistake.

entries.title: FAQ: What does it cost?
entries.text:
Kawase pays the network fee to set your wallet up and for payments inside your allowance. For payments you sign yourself,
a small USDC network fee is shown on the card. Bridges show the provider's fee before you confirm; swaps show the rate and
fees.

entries.title: FAQ: Which countries and currencies?
entries.text:
Kawase is built around USDC (dollars) and EURC (euros) on Arc, in ten languages. On mainnet you can also hold and
trade any token on Arc, and buy with a card where Circle's Onramp serves you. See what works today.

entries.title: FAQ: What happens to a payment if my phone dies mid-way?
entries.text:
Nothing is lost or doubled. Each payment is recorded before it is sent; Kawase keeps checking the network until it knows
the outcome, and only a receipt with the exact transfer marks it paid. Automations are claimed once per run and recovered
after a restart.

entries.title: FAQ: Can I use it without Kawase one day?
entries.text:
Yes. Your account is an ordinary account on Arc, and Settings → Account → Export wallet gives you its private key (shown by Privy's own window); see
Withdraw without Kawase.

entries.title: FAQ: Why does testnet exist in the app?
entries.text:
So you can try everything — sends, swaps, bridges, automations, voice — with free test money before using real money. The
header pill switches networks in one tap.

entries.title: FAQ: Is the code open?
entries.text:
The repository is Blockchain-Oracle/kawase on GitHub; it is being made public
for the hackathon submission.

entries.title: Automations
entries.text:
Automations are where an agent earns its keep: things that should happen without you opening the app. Every automation
runs unattended, but inside an on-chain grant you sign once, so even Kawase itself cannot make it do more.

entries.title: Automations: Scheduled payments
entries.text:
"Every Friday at 9 send 10 dollars to Alex." Kawase reads it back with the next runs and the maximum it could ever move,
then you turn it on with one Face ID. That signs the automation's own grant: it may only transfer that token, only
to Alex's address (pinned on chain), and only up to the amount per period. Schedules: every day, every week on a weekday,
or every month on day 1–28, in your own time zone.

Each run happens exactly once: if Kawase's server restarts mid-run, the run is recovered under the same id and never
paid twice. Weekly and monthly runs get a reminder a day before (with a heads-up when your wallet is short). A run
that can't go ahead is skipped with a reason in your inbox, and a run skipped for lack of money is retried once
when money arrives.

entries.title: Automations: Auto-save
entries.text:
"Keep 100 dollars in my wallet and save the rest." Auto-save keeps that amount ready and moves anything above it into your
own vault savings (see Earn). When your wallet drops below the line, it tops it back up from
savings. It checks daily and whenever money arrives. Its grants only allow moving USDC between your wallet and your own
savings, never anywhere else.

entries.title: Automations: DCA
entries.text:
- DCA ("buy 20 dollars of cirBTC every week") buys a token with a fixed amount on a schedule. Each run waits for you in
  Needs you with a fresh executable quote.

entries.title: Automations: Rules
entries.text:
"When my balance goes above 500, bridge what's above 400 to my Base address." A rule has:

- a trigger: the balance goes above or below an amount; money arrives (optionally from someone, or at least an
  amount); money goes out (round-ups); or a token's price crosses a level (checked on the executable quote every
  two minutes);
- an action: bridge USDC to your own address on another network (the route fee is capped on chain), save into your
  vault, send to someone (bounded on chain), swap, or just alert you;
- an amount: what is above a line, a share of the money that arrived, or a fixed amount.

A balance or price rule fires once per crossing and re-arms when it goes back. A round-up rule ("round up my
payments and save the change") saves the difference from each send into your own vault.

entries.title: Automations: Practice first
entries.text:
A new automation can start in practice: it runs without a grant, and each run is the exact transfer as a dry run on
Arc, recorded as "would have". Nothing moves. When you're happy, Go live signs its grant. Ask "what would happen if
this ran now?" for a dry run on demand. With global practice mode on, every
automation runs in practice.

entries.title: Automations: Needs you
entries.text:
An automation never swaps on its own, and never pays above its grant or past your allowlist or new-recipient rules. When a
run reaches such a step it waits in Needs you (inbox and Automations, with a push where notifications are set up).
Approving opens the same send or swap you'd make by hand. Unanswered items are reminded after 12 hours and expire after
24. See Needs you.

entries.title: Automations: Managing them
entries.text:
From the Automations screen or in chat: list, pause, resume, skip the next run, edit and cancel.

- Editing in place: asking for less applies at once; asking for more signs a new grant together with the old one's
  revoke.
- Cancelling also revokes the grant on chain, so the permission is gone, not just hidden.

entries.title: Bridge and withdraw
entries.text:
Ask Kawase ("send 20 dollars to Alex on Base", "bring my USDC from Base to Arc") and it puts a move card in front of
you, which also opens full screen as Move to another chain. It moves USDC between Arc and Base, Ethereum, Arbitrum,
Optimism, Polygon or Avalanche.

entries.title: Bridge and withdraw: Out of Arc, to anyone
entries.text:
The recipient can be you, a contact, an @handle or any 0x address. Kawase asks three providers for a live
quote:

- Circle CCTP: Circle burns the USDC on Arc and mints it on the other network;
- Across and Relay: a solver pays out on the other side, and is repaid from your deposit.

They are ranked by what arrives after fees, with ties going to the faster one. Up to three routes are shown with the
provider's mark, what arrives, the fee and the expected time. The best one is picked for you, and you can tap another.

Before your wallet is asked, Kawase builds the chosen provider's transaction and checks it: for Across it decodes the
deposit (who pays, who receives, which token, the amount, the minimum, the destination, no extra message); for Relay it
checks the approval and deposit into Relay's listed depository; for CCTP, Circle's own call checks. The transaction is
simulated from your wallet, then sent as one transaction after you slide and confirm with Face ID.

entries.title: Bridge and withdraw: Bring to Arc
entries.text:
If you hold USDC at the same address on another network, Kawase finds it (the balances are shown, the largest picked) and
brings it to Arc with Relay's permit: one signature, and no gas needed on that network. The permit is checked
(your address, the amount, Relay's contract and that network's USDC) before you sign.

entries.title: Bridge and withdraw: Following a move
entries.text:
Every move is tracked: Signed → Sent → Arriving → Delivered, with explorer links. Kawase checks the amount that left
your wallet on the receipt, then the fill through the provider's own status (Across deposit status, Relay request status
or Circle's attestation). If a provider refunds instead, the card says so plainly. Nothing is ever sent twice.

entries.title: Bridge and withdraw: On testnet
entries.text: Arc Testnet uses CCTP only; Across and Relay serve Arc mainnet. Bring to Arc is mainnet only.

entries.title: Bridge and withdraw: Withdraw
entries.text:
Withdraw (from Home, or "withdraw everything to my Kraken") takes one token, several or everything out of Kawase:

### What
Pick the tokens. Each one goes as itself or as cash (converted to USDC first).

### Where
An exchange (Kraken, Bybit, OKX, Binance, Bitget, KuCoin, or Coinbase through Base), your own wallet on Arc or
another chain, or your bank through an exchange. Kawase knows which assets and networks each exchange accepts and
warns you before you send something it would not credit. Places you withdraw to are saved in My places.

### One confirmation
Kawase plans a line per token: a transfer on Arc, a bridge, or a conversion first. You slide once and confirm with one
Face ID. A tracker follows every line to the end; if something stops half way, Finish it picks up where it was.

Tokens other than USDC cross chains as USDC (converted first). On testnet, exchanges aren't offered; withdraw goes to your
own wallet. In the exit kit, "move the money out" opens Withdraw for everything.

To take your money out without Kawase at all, follow Withdraw without Kawase.

entries.title: Buy with Apple Pay or card
entries.text:
"Buy 50 dollars of USDC", or Add money → Buy with Apple Pay or card (the first row).

### Choose the amount
Pick a preset or type an amount, in dollars or euros. The sheet shows the payment methods Circle offers and says plainly
whether this is real money (mainnet) or Circle's sandbox (testnet, test cards only).

### Pay at Circle
Buy opens Circle's checkout full screen (where Apple Pay works). Kawase creates the session on its server, for your
own address on Arc.

### Funded
Back in Kawase, the order is followed until the chain confirms the delivery, then you see "You're funded". If the
payment didn't complete, Circle's reason is shown with Try again.

entries.title: Buy with Apple Pay or card: Buying another token
entries.text:
Ask for any other token ("buy 30 dollars of cirBTC with Apple Pay") and Kawase buys USDC first, then opens the swap for
what arrived, with one more approval and both fees shown. It only ever continues to a canonical or listed token, never a
look-alike.

entries.title: Buy with Apple Pay or card: Where it runs
entries.text:
- Mainnet: Circle's production Onramp with real cards. Apple Pay and Google Pay appear once Circle finishes its
  business check of Kawase's domain; the checkout shows which methods it offers.
- Testnet: Circle's Onramp sandbox with test cards. No real money moves. The free
  faucet works too.

Selling to a bank account isn't built. To cash out, send to an exchange that accepts Arc deposits (see
Withdraw without Kawase).

entries.title: Contacts and @handles: Contacts
entries.text:
A contact is a name (and nicknames) with one or more addresses. Kawase uses contacts to understand "send to Alex" and to
protect you:

- Address changes are held. When a contact's address changes, the new address waits 24 hours before money can go to
  it, and the contact is frozen meanwhile. A changed address is a classic way to steal a payment.
- Look-alike addresses are flagged. An address whose first and last four characters match one of your contacts' is
  treated as a look-alike: Kawase stops and asks for Face ID.
- Payment history builds trust per address and per network: a first payment to an address is treated more carefully
  than a repeat one.

If you mention someone Kawase doesn't know, it asks you to save them and then carries on with the same payment — you don't
have to start over.

### Adding people

- Save a sender: money that arrived from someone offers Save sender as a contact, with the address from the
  payment.
- Import from your phone: Contacts → Import reads names and emails on your phone only. Find who's on Kawase
  sends only hashed emails, never the names, emails or numbers themselves; people who allow being found are added by their
  @handle in one tap, and you can invite the rest. Whether others can find you this way is a switch on the same page.

entries.title: Contacts and @handles: @handles
entries.text:
A @handle is an optional public name you can be paid by: "send 10 to @abu". Rules:

- 3 to 20 characters: lowercase letters, digits and underscore.
- Unique regardless of case; names that would impersonate Kawase, Arc, Circle or staff are reserved.
- You choose it during onboarding (or skip) and can change it in Settings.

A handle resolves to the person's Kawase wallet address. If the person hasn't set up a wallet yet, Kawase tells you
instead of guessing.

entries.title: Earn and borrow: Yield options
entries.text:
"Where can my 200 dollars earn?" Kawase compares every source that takes your asset, from live reads:

- Aave V4 supply: the current rate, how much the market could pay out right now, and its size;
- Morpho vaults listed by Circle's App Kit Earn, ranked by what they could give back now. A vault that couldn't return
  your money is never offered, and low liquidity is flagged;
- Aero liquidity campaigns from Merkl: shown as advanced, read only.

Options are ranked by rate among the sources that could return your amount, with the best one marked. Tapping Aave opens
the supply ticket; tapping a vault opens Earn for that vault.

entries.title: Earn and borrow: Earn with Morpho vaults
entries.text:
"Put 50 dollars in savings", or the Earn screen. Deposit USDC into the vault you pick (or the best active one) and
withdraw any amount back. Your positions are read live from the vaults. Each deposit or withdrawal is one Face ID,
sent as one transaction. Auto-save uses the same vaults by itself.

On testnet, Earn uses Arc Testnet's mock Morpho vaults.

entries.title: Earn and borrow: Borrow and supply on Aave V4
entries.text:
The Borrow screen (from Earn on mainnet) shows your Aave V4 position first: what you owe (with Repay), what you
supplied (with Add and Withdraw), the health gauge and how much room is left. Then what you can borrow, and at
what rate.

- Borrow USDC, EURC, cirBTC or WETH against collateral of USDC, cirBTC or WETH. EURC can't be collateral on Aave V4.
  Kawase picks the collateral from your wallet (the held asset worth most after its factor) and puts it in in the same
  transaction.
- The gauge moves with every digit you type. Max keeps you at the safe floor.
- A loan that would leave health under 1.25 is refused; under 1.5 you're warned.
- With one collateral asset, the ticket shows the price at which it would be liquidated.
- Repay part or all. "All" repays everything with a small margin for interest, and resets the approval.

Every action is re-checked against fresh prices when you approve, simulated from your wallet, and sent as one
transaction. You confirm by sliding and Face ID.

entries.title: Earn and borrow: Not on testnet
entries.text: Aave V4 is on Arc mainnet only, so borrowing and Aave supply are too. Morpho vaults work on both networks.

entries.title: Ten languages
entries.text:
Kawase speaks the world's most widely spoken languages, everywhere in the app:

| Language | Name in the language | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| English | English | left to right |
| Chinese | 中文 | left to right |
| Hindi | हिन्दी | left to right |
| Spanish | Español | left to right |
| French | Français | left to right |
| Arabic | العربية | right to left |
| Bengali | বাংলা | left to right |
| Portuguese | Português | left to right |
| Russian | Русский | left to right |
| Urdu | اردو | right to left |

- From the first screen. The language pill is on the first onboarding panel and every screen after it; changing it is
  instant, direction included.
- Every string in every language. The app's ten catalogs are complete; the agent replies in your language and
  voice hears and speaks all ten.
- Amounts stay exact. Numbers are formatted for your language, while amounts, addresses and codes stay left-to-right
  so they can be checked character by character.
- These docs are available in the same ten languages (use the language switch in the sidebar).

entries.title: Limits and control
entries.text:
Everything the agent may do without asking is written down in Settings → Wallet & limits, and most of it is enforced
by Arc itself. This page shows what you can change there. The model behind it is on the safety page.

entries.title: Limits and control: Your allowance, per token
entries.text:
The authority receipt shows, for each token, what Arc enforces (the grant you signed) and Kawase's own lower cap, what
is left today, and any temporary raise.

- Add a token: any token you hold, or an address you paste, checked on chain.
- Lower a number and it saves at once.
- Raise one and you see Now → After: one approval signs the new on-chain grant together with the revoke of the
  old one, so two grants are never live at the same time.

entries.title: Limits and control: What Kawase checks on its own
Limits and control: The brake
Limits and control: Token rules
entries.text:
Wallet & limits → Token rules sets which tokens Kawase may buy for you: verified only, or verified and popular
ones with warnings; caps for unverified tokens per trade and per day, with today's meter; and the highest price impact you
accept. Copycats and high-risk tokens are always blocked. Tightening applies at once; loosening asks for Face ID and your
wallet's signature.

entries.title: Limits and control: Pause all
entries.text:
One switch turns off everything the agent does without asking: no payment uses the allowance (each one waits for your
Face ID), every automation run is skipped, and the agent buys nothing in the marketplace. What you do yourself still
works, swaps, bridges and withdrawals included, so you can always move your money out. While paused, a strip sits above
every screen.

entries.title: Limits and control: The risk dial
entries.text:
Guard · Balanced · Autonomous:

- Guard: every payment waits for your confirmation, chat too.
- Balanced: inside your allowance, a typed request goes at once.
- Autonomous: Kawase may act on its own suggestions inside your limits, then tells you.

entries.title: Limits and control: Practice mode
entries.text:
With practice on, Kawase runs the exact transaction you asked for as a dry run on Arc, from your own address, and shows
"Would have sent" with the chain's answer. Nothing moves. Practice also covers automations, and a marketplace
purchase answers "would pay" with the live price and nothing paid. Swaps, bridges, savings moves and margin orders are
refused before anything is signed, so the PRACTICE strip never hides a real payment.

entries.title: Limits and control: The exit kit
entries.text:
If something feels wrong: pause, then hold to revoke every permission on the network with one Face ID (one
transaction), then move the money out, which opens Withdraw for everything.
Automations whose grants are revoked end.

entries.title: Limits and control: Needs you
entries.text:
Some steps an automation may never take alone: every swap, a payment above its grant, or one your allowlist or
cooldown holds back. They wait in Needs you, in the inbox and in Automations, with a push notification where
notifications are set up. Answer from anywhere, once: a second answer finds it already answered and says when and where.
Approving opens the very send or swap you would make by hand, re-checked. Unanswered items are reminded after 12
hours and expire after 24.

entries.title: Limits and control: Activity and why
entries.text:
Activity is one feed of every token in and out: sends, receives, swaps with both legs, bridges, savings, margin,
automation runs, requests paid, the faucet and practice runs. Each row says where it stands (checking, skipped and why,
practice, waiting). Filters: All · In · Out · Trades · Automations · Needs you, the last with its count.

Tap a row for its receipt (amount, time, network, the other side, the transaction), then Why: the decision record
behind it, or for a run that never reached the chain, what stopped it and how you answered. From Activity you can also
read the week's report and export your history as CSV or beancount.

entries.title: Limits and control: From chat
entries.text:
Ask "what are my limits?", "pause everything", "set the dial to guard", "raise my USDC allowance to 50" or "revoke
everything". Each answer is a card, and changes are approved on the card.

entries.title: Long and short
entries.text:
Kawase Margin lets you bet on a price going up (long) or down (short) with more than you put in. It runs on
Aave V4 on Arc mainnet, through your own Aave account: no exchange account, no flash loan, and nothing held by
Kawase.

entries.title: Long and short: How a position is built
entries.text:
- Long X: your USDC margin is swapped to X and supplied as collateral, then Kawase borrows USDC against it, swaps it to
  more X and supplies that, a few times in a loop.
- Short X: your USDC is supplied as collateral, then Kawase borrows X, swaps it to USDC and supplies that, in a loop.
- Closing runs it backwards: withdraw, swap, repay, then the rest comes back to your wallet.

The whole position opens or closes as one transaction from your own wallet (an EIP-7702 batch). The swap legs come from
KyberSwap with checked calldata. Each loop borrows only down to a safe health at oracle prices, and the account opens at a
health of 1.10 or more.

entries.title: Long and short: Markets
entries.text:
Markets come from Aave V4's live reserves on Arc. Today:

- cirBTC (Circle's Bitcoin) and WETH: long and short;
- EURC: short only, because EURC can't be collateral on Aave V4.

Leverage is capped by each asset's collateral factor. At today's factors that is about 3.4× long cirBTC, 4× long
WETH and 2.4× for a short. Margin is paid in USDC.

entries.title: Long and short: The ticket
Long and short: Positions
entries.text:
Each position has its own page: profit and loss split into price and borrowing cost, a health gauge, its
liquidation price, and Close 25% · 50% · 75% · All, which drafts the unwind into the same ticket. Home's For you
card warns you when an open position's health drops under 1.25 or liquidation is within a 10% move.

entries.title: Long and short: Not on testnet
entries.text: Aave V4 is on Arc mainnet only, so Kawase Margin is too. On testnet the screen explains this and offers the switch.

entries.title: Agent wallet and marketplace
entries.text:
x402 is an open standard for paying for a web request with stablecoins: the service answers "402 Payment Required"
with a price, the client pays in USDC and gets the result. Kawase uses it to buy answers for you: web search and news,
prediction-market odds, DefiLlama yields and prices, stock prices, data enrichment, from Circle's x402 catalog on Arc.

entries.title: Agent wallet and marketplace: Your agent wallet
entries.text:
Purchases never come out of your main wallet directly. Kawase has a separate agent wallet for you, and it can only
spend what you put in:

- Top up from your Kawase wallet with a preset. The first top-up signs a capped marketplace grant with Face ID;
  later top-ups need no prompt, inside that cap. Or top up with Apple Pay or a card through Circle's Onramp, straight
  into the agent wallet.
- Its balance is split between Circle Gateway (ready for nanopayments, which most sellers take) and a part on hand
  for sellers that take plain USDC (EIP-3009). When a plain-USDC purchase needs more on hand, Kawase refills it from
  Gateway itself.
- Return to my wallet sends both parts back at any time.

Settings → Agent wallet shows the balance, what was spent today, the address and the full history of purchases and
moves.

entries.title: Agent wallet and marketplace: Budgets you set
Agent wallet and marketplace: Every purchase receipted
entries.text:
Chat shows what Kawase found (the seller's mark, what it returns and the price) and, after paying, a receipt: "Paid 0.002
USDC to …". The seller's answer is labelled unchecked. x402 has no refund standard yet: if a call fails after payment,
the receipt says the seller kept it; a payment that Circle reports as failed is marked not charged. Kawase treats outside text as data, never as instructions, and
says so when an answer tries to tell it what to do.

entries.title: Agent wallet and marketplace: Networks
entries.text:
- Mainnet: Circle's catalog (about 2,100 listings on Arc), paid over both rails.
- Testnet: Circle's catalog has no testnet listings, so Kawase runs its own demo seller (seller.getkawase.xyz) to
  try it end to end with test money.

entries.title: Memory and search: Memory
entries.text:
"Remember that my landlord is @maria." Kawase keeps facts you ask it to remember (people, @handles, preferences) and
uses them later. When an answer relies on one, chat shows a From memory line, so you always know where it came from.

Settings → Memory lists every fact: add one, edit it, forget one or all, or turn memory off. A guest's memory moves
into the account on sign-in. Kawase doesn't remember things you didn't ask it to.

entries.title: Memory and search: Search every conversation
entries.text:
The history sheet searches all your conversations on Kawase's server, not just the ones loaded: the words, the cards
and who they were for (search "Maria" and the send to her shows up). Partial words and Chinese, Japanese or Korean text
work. Results are grouped by conversation with the words around the match, and open the conversation. You can also ask:
"what did I send my landlord last month?"

entries.title: Memory and search: Long conversations
entries.text:
A long thread stays coherent: after each turn, the older part is folded into a summary and the latest messages are kept
word for word. The summary never restates amounts or outcomes from memory; the cards' own results are kept exactly as they
were, and Kawase checks again with its tools before relying on one.

entries.title: Memory and search: For you
Memory and search: Answers about Arc, with sources
entries.text:
Ask "how fast is finality on Arc?" or "what does a transfer cost?". Kawase answers from a curated set of notes built from
Arc's and Circle's documentation and these docs, and shows a Sources card naming each one. Facts only, no investment
advice.

entries.title: Memory and search: Cards that explain
entries.text:
- Charts: your portfolio's value, or any token's price, over a day, a week, a month or a year.
- Why this one?: why a bridge route, swap venue or vault won (every provider asked, what each delivers, the fee and the
  time, why the others lost or couldn't quote).
- Settings changes as Now → After, applied on your device (memory on or off, reply language, theme).
- Status: whether Kawase, Arc (each network), Circle and prices are up, slow or down.

entries.title: Memory and search: Outside text is data
entries.text:
Anything Kawase reads from outside (marketplace answers, token and vault names, chain memos, contact notes, past messages)
is fenced as untrusted. Instructions hidden in it are flagged and never followed.

entries.title: The network toggle
entries.text:
Kawase works on two networks: Arc mainnet, where money is real, and Arc testnet, where it is not. The network
pill in the header switches between them in one tap, both ways, like dark mode.

- New accounts start on testnet, and anything missing or unreadable falls back to testnet: the safe direction.
- The first switch to mainnet shows a short "Real money" consent; after that it is instant.
- Always visible, never colour alone. On testnet a strip says "Testnet · no real money"; on mainnet, money cards carry a
  REAL MONEY label. The pill names the network, and the voice orb changes colour (lime on mainnet, sky blue on
  testnet).
- Your wallet is the same on both: one address, the same contacts and settings. Balances and activity are per network.
- The server decides. The network is part of your session on the server, never chosen by the AI model; every payment
  carries the network it was prepared for, and a mismatch stops it.

When something exists on only one network — the faucet on testnet, the x402 marketplace on mainnet — Kawase says so and
offers to switch rather than failing. See networks for the full comparison.

entries.title: Notifications
entries.text:
Kawase's inbox is the record: every payment received, request paid, payment completed, automation skipped and rule
alert lands there, and tapping one opens the right screen.

On top of the inbox, Kawase can tell you by push (on your phone) and email. In Settings → Notifications you choose,
per event and per channel, what reaches you. The defaults:

| Event | Push | Email |
|---|---|---|
| Money received | on | on |
| Your request was paid | on | on |
| Your payment completed | on | off |
| An automation was skipped | on | on |
| A rule alert | on | on |

Quiet hours in your own time zone hold push notifications until morning; email still goes. Security events can never
be muted.

Each notification is delivered at most once per channel, even if Kawase retries. Push and email delivery are built into
the app and the server; they switch on as the push (Apple and Google) and email provider accounts are connected for the
public release. The inbox works today.

entries.title: Send, receive and request: Send
entries.text:
Say or type who and how much ("send 20 dollars to Alex", "pay @mira 5 euros"), or use the Send screen. You can send any
token you hold on Arc. Kawase:

1. Finds the recipient: a saved contact, a Kawase @handle, an 0x… address you typed yourself, or a QR code you
   scanned. The agent can only use an address that came from your contacts, a code you scanned, or your own message, word
   for word.
2. Picks the token you hold, or asks if it is unclear.
3. Checks the recipient on every payment: a token contract or a look-alike of a saved contact is refused, a contract
   that isn't a wallet is warned about, the token issuer's blocklist is checked where it has one, and your own address is
   named as yours. It also checks your balance, your limits and whether a contact's address changed recently.
4. Shows the payment card with the exact amount, token, recipient and network.

Then one of two things happens:

| Situation | What you do |
|---|---|
| Inside what is left of today's allowance for that token, to someone you have paid before or named in this request | Nothing. It is sent at once and Kawase says so. |
| Above the allowance, a token outside it, a new address, or a look-alike address | Confirm with Face ID (fingerprint or screen lock on Android, an email code on the web). |

A payment to an address you just added can suggest sending a test amount first. A payment is only marked…

entries.title: Send, receive and request: Scan to pay
entries.text:
Tap Scan in the quick-action fan, on Send, or in chat's header. The scanner reads:

- a bare address, or a payment link with an amount and token (EIP-681): Send opens filled in, and the usual checks run;
- a Kawase request link: its pay page opens.

A code for the other Arc network, another chain or a closed request says why, with a network switch where that helps. You
can also paste a code instead.

entries.title: Send, receive and request: Receive and add money
Send, receive and request: Request and split
entries.text:
"Request 15 dollars from Sam for dinner", or open Request. Kawase creates a payment request in any token on Arc with a
shareable link. The person paying can open it in any browser; the request is marked paid when a Kawase payment or a
matching plain transfer arrives.

Split a bill: "split 30 dollars for dinner with Amina and Tunde". Equal shares or by hand, with you included or not.
Each person gets their own request and link, and a progress card shows who has paid.

entries.title: Send, receive and request: Receipts and links
entries.text:
- Share a receipt of a finished payment as an image card (or text with the explorer link on the web).
- Every action has its own link (/i/…). Notifications open the exact card; a link opened while signed out comes back to
  it after sign-in. A card blocked by something you then fix (sign in, setup, limits, adding money) checks again by itself.

entries.title: Trade any token: Markets
entries.text:
The Markets tab (in the dock, between Home and the orb) is open to guests too:

- Search by name, symbol or contract address.
- Segments Trending · Meme · Long/Short · Stocks & FX · New, a carousel of hot markets, and a heatmap where each
  tile is sized by the day's volume and coloured by its move.
- Rows show the price, the day's change, volume and liquidity. A token that copies another one carries a copycat
  chip; fakes stay flagged in the list and never reach the carousel or the heatmap.

Markets are an Arc mainnet thing. On testnet the tab says so and offers the switch.

entries.title: Trade any token: A page for every token
Trade any token: Your portfolio, every token
Trade any token: Buy, sell or swap any pair
entries.text:
"Buy 20 dollars of ARGUS", "sell half my cirBTC", or the ticket from a token page. You pay with any token you hold
and get any token (search by name, symbol or address). For every trade Kawase asks three venues at once, KyberSwap,
Circle's App Kit and LI.FI, and recommends the one that delivers the most. The others are listed with what they would
deliver, or why they couldn't quote.

The review shows the amount you get at least, the price impact against the market price and the route. You confirm by
sliding on the card, then Face ID. Only the chosen venue builds the transaction, at half the slippage you were
shown, and Kawase checks its calls (router, amounts, recipient, the on-chain minimum) before your wallet is asked. The
approval and the trade go out as one transaction from your own wallet.

entries.title: Trade any token: Token rules
Trade any token: On testnet
entries.text:
Arc Testnet has only USDC ↔ EURC to trade, through the same ticket. Every other token, and meme coins, are mainnet
only.

Long and short positions have their own page: Long and short.

entries.title: Voice
entries.text:
Tap the orb in the dock and speak. The page blurs, the orb rises and listens; it shows the words it heard, answers aloud,
and puts the same cards on screen as chat does.

- One conversation. What you said by voice is in your chat thread, and typing picks it up where you left off.
- Captions on both sides: what Kawase heard, and what it is saying.
- A spoken "yes" never approves a payment. A send by voice is prepared on its card and waits for your tap and Face ID
  (fingerprint or screen lock on Android) — even inside your daily allowance.
- Mute with one tap: nothing is heard or sent while muted. Type instead is always there.
- The orb shows the network: lime on mainnet, sky blue on testnet.

entries.title: Voice: On the web
entries.text:
Voice works in the web app too: allow the microphone when the browser asks. If you refuse it, or there is no microphone,
Kawase stays connected, says how to allow it, and typing is right beside it. Kawase's own voice still plays.

entries.title: Voice: Settings → Voice
entries.text:
- Kawase's voice: one of six.
- Speaking speed: relaxed, normal or brisk.
- Kawase speaks first: it greets you as soon as voice opens; turned off, it waits for you.

Changes apply the next time you start talking.

entries.title: Voice: How it works
entries.text:
The phone or browser joins a LiveKit room over WebRTC, and Kawase's voice worker joins the same room. Every money or
account request is handed to the same agent turn as chat (same tools, same limits, same thread); the cards arrive on
your screen while the answer is spoken. Before speaking amounts, assets, @handles or the network, the worker checks them
against what the tools returned and corrects a mismatch. If the realtime voice can't start, Kawase falls back to a
listen → answer → speak pipeline with the same agent behind it. LiveKit doesn't record the conversation.

entries.title: Web and desktop: In the browser
entries.text:
Open app.getkawase.xyz. You start as a guest, and everything works as on the phone:
chat, cards, Markets, voice and every screen.

- Confirming a payment: an email code stands in for Face ID.
- Voice: tap the orb and allow the microphone when the browser asks. If you refuse it, Kawase says how to allow it, and
  typing is right there.
- Install it: Kawase is an installable web app. In Chrome or Edge use Install, in Safari Add to Dock (Mac) or
  Add to Home Screen (iPhone). If the network drops, an offline page says so instead of a broken screen. Kawase never
  caches balances, so nothing old is ever shown as current money.

entries.title: Web and desktop: The desktop app (Mac)
Web and desktop: On the phone
entries.text: Kawase for iPhone is on TestFlight and for Android as an APK. See getting started.

entries.title: Getting started: 1. Open the app
entries.text:
Open app.getkawase.xyz in any modern browser. You start as a guest: no sign-up, no
    email. You can chat with Kawase, talk to it, look around every screen and see what it would do.

    On the web, an email code stands in for Face ID wherever a payment needs your confirmation. You can install the
    web app, or use the desktop app for Mac.
  
  
    Kawase for iPhone is distributed through TestFlight while it is in beta. Install TestFlight from the App Store,
    then open the invite link you were given. A public TestFlight link will be published on the showcase page when it is
    available.
  
  
    Download the Android build (APK) from Expo:
    build e644e19d.
    Open it on the phone and allow the install. On Android the confirmation is your fingerprint or screen lock.

entries.title: Getting started: 2. Pick your language
entries.text:
The language pill is on the very first screen. Kawase speaks ten languages, and Arabic and
Urdu switch the whole layout to right-to-left at once. You can change it again at any time in Settings.

entries.title: Getting started: 3. Sign in when you want to keep things
entries.text:
Guests can explore everything. To hold money, sign in with:

- an email code,
- Apple, or
- Google.

There is no password and no PIN. Signing in creates your wallet (see safety): one address that works on
both networks. Everything you did as a guest — your chat, your contacts — moves into your account.

Setting the wallet up costs you nothing: you sign one authorization and Kawase pays the network fee.

entries.title: Getting started: 4. Get test money
entries.text:
New accounts start on testnet, where money has no value. Ask Kawase "get me test money" or open the faucet from the
home screen. Each claim brings about 20 test USDC and 20 test EURC from Circle's faucet, once a day. If the in-app
claim is refused, Circle's own faucet is at faucet.circle.com (choose "Arc Testnet").

entries.title: Getting started: 5. Accept your daily allowance
entries.text:
Kawase asks you once to accept an everyday allowance: an amount of USDC per day that the agent may send for you without
asking again. You approve it with one Face ID. The default is shown on the card before you approve; see the
limits table.

entries.title: Getting started: 6. Make your first payment
entries.text:
Type or say, for example (use a friend's @handle, or paste the address of a second wallet of your own):

> send 1 dollar to @friend

Kawase finds the recipient, checks your balance and limits, and shows the payment card: exact amount, currency, recipient
and network. Inside your allowance it sends at once; above it, it waits for your Face ID. The card follows the payment
until the network confirms it, and the receipt links to the block explorer.

entries.title: Getting started: 7. Try the rest
entries.text:
- "swap 2 dollars to euros"
- "move 1 dollar to Base"
- "put 5 dollars in savings"
- "every Friday at 9 send 1 dollar to Alex"
- "keep 20 dollars in my wallet and save the rest"
- "buy 10 dollars of USDC with a card" (Circle's sandbox on testnet)
- "remember that Alex is my brother"

On mainnet, Markets, trading any token, long and short, and borrowing are there too. See the features.

Each one shows a card first and tells you exactly what it needs from you.

entries.title: What Kawase is
entries.text:
Kawase (為替, "exchange" in Japanese) is a money app with an AI agent at its centre, built for Arc, Circle's stablecoin
network. You tell it what you want — "send 20 dollars to Alex", "swap half my euros to dollars", "every Friday put 10
dollars aside" — by voice or by typing, in any of ten languages. Kawase works out the details, shows you exactly what will
happen, and does it.

entries.title: What Kawase is: One app for everything on Arc
entries.text:
The goal is that anything a person can do with money on Arc, they can do by asking Kawase:

- Send, receive and request any token, to a saved contact, a Kawase @handle,
  any address or a scanned QR code; split a bill with a link per person.
- Withdraw any token to an exchange, your own wallet on another chain,
  or your bank through an exchange, confirmed once.
- Trade any token: Markets, a page with safety checks for every token, and any pair at
  the best of KyberSwap, Circle's App Kit and LI.FI, meme coins included (mainnet).
- Long and short with Kawase Margin on Aave V4 (mainnet).
- Buy with a card, Apple Pay or Google Pay through Circle's Onramp.
- Bridge USDC to anyone on six networks over Circle CCTP, Across or Relay, ranked
  by what arrives, and bring USDC to Arc with no gas on the other chain.
- Earn and borrow: yield options across Aave V4, Morpho vaults and Aero; borrowing on
  Aave V4 with a health gauge.
- Automations: scheduled payments, Auto-save, DCA and rules, each bounded on chain,
  with practice runs first.
- The agent wallet: Kawase pays for services per call over x402, inside a budget.
- Limits and control: your allowance per token, Pause all, practice mode, the exit
  kit and Needs you.
- Memory and search, suggestions on Home, and answers about Arc with sources.
- Voice on iPhone, Android and the web, and the whole app in ten languages, in the browser…

entries.title: What Kawase is: Why an agent, and why it is safe
entries.text:
Most money apps make you find the right screen. Kawase lets you say what you mean, and the agent fills in the rest: who
"Alex" is, which currency you hold, which route is cheapest. What it can never do is move money beyond what you allowed:

- Inside your daily allowance the agent just sends and tells you — no prompt. The allowance is an on-chain limit you
  signed once; the chain refuses anything above it.
- Above the allowance, for a new recipient over a threshold, a look-alike address, a swap or a bridge, you confirm with
  Face ID (fingerprint or screen lock on Android, an email code on the web).
- Automations run unattended, but each one is pinned on chain to its recipient and amount per period.

Read the safety model for the details.

entries.title: What Kawase is: Two networks, one tap
entries.text:
Kawase runs on Arc mainnet (real money) and Arc testnet (test money, free from the in-app faucet). New accounts
start on testnet. The network pill in the header switches between them in one tap, like dark mode; the app, the orb and
every money card always say which one you are on. See networks.

entries.title: What Kawase is: Where to try it
entries.text:
- Web app, no install, starts as a guest: app.getkawase.xyz
- Mac: the desktop app
- iPhone (TestFlight) and Android (APK): see getting started.

entries.title: Judge walkthrough
entries.text:
This page is for reviewers who click around without us in the room. Each step says what to do, what you should see, and
where the proof is: the demo page groups every real Arc testnet transaction behind a claim,
and each step links to its group (for example /demo#send). Testnet money has no
value, so nothing here costs anything.

- Chat and voice are paused: the AI model provider's prepaid credit has run out.
- Mainnet moves no money yet: Kawase's mainnet relayer has not been funded.

Until these are lifted, the steps marked paused below cannot be run on the live app; their transactions on the demo
page are the proof that they work.

entries.title: Judge walkthrough: What you can try right now
entries.text:
Use app.getkawase.xyz in a desktop or phone browser, the
Android APK, or
TestFlight if you have an invite.

1. Arrive as a guest. Pick a language from the pill on the first screen (Arabic and Urdu turn the whole layout
   right-to-left), swipe the short story, and open every screen: Home, Markets, a token page, Activity, Settings.
2. Help & trust (Settings): what Kawase can do, where your money lives, how to leave without Kawase, and the live
   state of Arc, Circle and prices.
3. Sign in with an email code (or Apple or Google). Kawase creates your own wallet with Privy: one address on both
   networks.
4. Get test money from the faucet card on Home: Circle's faucet sends about 20 USDC and 20 EURC. Your balance,
   the fee chip ("~N actions left": Arc's fees are paid in USDC) and the receive page with your QR code follow.
5. Switch networks with the pill in the header: the first switch to mainnet shows the real-money consent.
6. Check the chain. Every claim below has a transaction on /demo that opens on the
   explorer.

entries.title: Judge walkthrough: The five-minute path (testnet, paused)
entries.text:
This is the path once chat and wallet signing are back. On the web an email code stands in for Face ID; on iPhone and
Android the same steps use Face ID or the fingerprint.

### 1. Ask what it can do

> what can you do?

You get the capability card: what works on testnet and on mainnet, from the same registry the agent reads before it
proposes anything (availability).

Proof: the demo video.

### 2. Set up the wallet and accept the allowance

Kawase upgrades your wallet in place with EIP-7702; you sign once and Kawase's relayer pays the fee. Then you accept the
everyday allowance with one confirmation: a delegation that lets Kawase's agent wallet send up to a daily amount of
USDC for you, with the cap, the token, the function, the redeemer and the expiry written on chain.

Proof: setup paid by the relayer, sends inside the on-chain
allowance.

### 3. Send money

> send 1 dollar to 0x… (paste an address you control, or a friend's @handle)

Kawase resolves the recipient, runs its checks (balance, limits, look-alike and contract addresses) and shows the card:
amount, currency, recipient, network. Inside the allowance it goes at once and the card follows the transaction to the
explorer; above it, or to a new address above the first-time threshold, it waits for your confirmation. A wallet with no
USDC left for fees still sends USDC or EURC: you sign once and the relayer pays.

Proof…

entries.title: Judge walkthrough: The mainnet path
entries.text:
Mainnet is real money, so it takes an account and an explicit consent. Tap the network pill: the first switch shows the
real-money consent; after it, the pill, the REAL MONEY label and the orb's colour all say mainnet. Your address is the
same; balances, history and limits are kept per network (network toggle).

What only mainnet has, each built against mainnet contracts and live quotes:

- Markets: every token on Arc with price, chart and safety checks; meme coins; a token still on a launchpad's bonding

- Long and short: Kawase Margin opens a leveraged position through your own Aave V4 account, with the liquidation
  price on the ticket before you slide (long and short).
- Earn and borrow: Aave V4 supply and borrowing with a live health gauge next to Morpho vaults and Aero campaigns
  (earn and borrow).
- Agent wallet: paid x402 services from Circle's catalog, inside a daily budget you set

entries.text:
The repository's README maps every feature to its package, and architecture lists the tests that
ran against Arc testnet. The availability page is generated from the capability registry

entries.title: Networks: How Kawase keeps them apart
entries.text:
- One tap to switch, both ways: see the network toggle.
- The network is shown three ways: the header pill, the testnet strip or the REAL MONEY label, and the orb's colour.
- The server owns the choice. Every payment is prepared for one network and carries it to the end; if the network
  changes in between, the payment stops instead of crossing over.
- One wallet address on both networks, with balances, activity and limits kept per network.

entries.title: Safety model
entries.text:
Kawase lets an AI move money for you. That only works if what it can do is small, visible and enforced by the
network — not by trust in the AI or in Kawase's servers. This page describes how.

entries.title: Safety model: Your wallet
entries.text:
- When you sign in (email code, Apple or Google), Kawase creates an ordinary Ethereum-style account (an EOA) whose key
  is held by Privy, split up in secure enclaves so that no single party ever holds it whole. There is no PIN and no
  password. It is one address on both networks.
- Kawase then upgrades that same account in place with EIP-7702, pointing its code at MetaMask's audited
  EIP7702StatelessDeleGator. You sign one authorization; Kawase's relayer sends it and pays the fee, so setup costs you
  nothing.
- After the upgrade your account can grant delegations (ERC-7710, from MetaMask's Delegation Framework): narrow,
  signed permissions with limits built in. Those are the only way the agent can ever move your money without you.

entries.title: Safety model: Two ways a payment is authorized
entries.text:
| | Inside your everyday allowance | Everything else |
|---|---|---|
| What it covers | USDC payments up to what is left of today's allowance, to someone you've paid before or named in this request | Above the allowance, any EURC payment, a first payment to a new address above the threshold, look-alike addresses, every swap, bridge and vault move, any change to your limits |
| What you do | Nothing. Kawase sends and tells you. | Face ID (fingerprint or screen lock on Android; an email code on the web) |
| What enforces it | The chain: your signed allowance delegation | Your signature over the exact transaction |

### The everyday allowance

You accept it once, with one Face ID, during setup. It is a delegation from your account to Kawase's agent wallet with
these limits written into it — decoded from the signed bytes and shown to you as a receipt before you sign:

- Token: USDC only, and only its transfer function.
- Amount: up to the daily allowance per 24-hour period (an on-chain period cap).
- Who may use it: only Kawase's agent wallet (a redeemer lock). A copy of the permission is useless to anyone else.
- Expiry: 90 days, after which it is dead and you accept a new one.
- No native value: nothing in it allows sending the network's gas token.

The chain refuses anything outside those limits — a larger amount, another token, another function, after expiry or after
you revoke…

entries.title: Safety model: Automations: pinned on chain
entries.text:
Each automation gets its own grant, signed with one Face ID when you turn it on:

- Scheduled payments: transfer only, pinned to one recipient, at most the amount per period, expiring when the
  automation ends.
- Auto-save: may only move USDC between your wallet and your own vault savings.
- Bridge rules: may only bridge USDC to your own address, with the route fee capped.

Cancelling an automation revokes its grant on chain in the same step.

entries.title: Safety model: What the agent can never do
entries.text:
- Move more than your allowance in a day, or use the allowance for anything other than a USDC transfer.
- Send to a recipient other than the one an automation's grant is pinned to.
- Swap, bridge, pay in EURC, pay a look-alike address or raise your limits without your Face ID.
- Approve a payment because of a spoken "yes": voice payments always wait for your tap.
- Invent an address: addresses come only from your contacts or from your own message, word for word.
- Choose the network: that is part of your session on the server, and every payment is checked against it.
- Mark something as paid without proof: only a receipt with the exact transfer counts. An unclear outcome is shown as
  "still checking" and never retried automatically, so nothing is paid twice.

entries.title: Safety model: Default limits
entries.text:
On top of the on-chain allowance, Kawase's policy engine checks your limits before anything is prepared (two taps at once
cannot both fit under the same limit):

entries.title: Safety model: Revoke and pause
entries.text:
- Revoke the allowance: Wallet & limits → Revoke (press and hold to confirm). It is one ordinary transaction from your
  wallet that disables the delegation on chain; the agent can no longer send anything without your Face ID.
- Pause, skip or cancel any automation from the Automations screen or in chat; cancelling revokes its grant.
- Pause all in Wallet & limits turns off everything the agent does without asking; your own Face ID payments still
  work. The exit kit pauses, revokes every permission in one transaction and helps you move the money out. See
  Limits and control.
- Leave entirely: see Withdraw without Kawase.

entries.title: Safety model: Proof
entries.text:
Every step above was run on Arc testnet with real transactions; the evidence table with explorer links is on the
showcase's demo page, and the architecture page lists the tests.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase
entries.text:
Kawase never holds your money. Your tokens sit in your own account on Arc, and the permissions you gave the agent are
narrow and expire on their own. This guide takes you out step by step: first with Kawase's help, then without it.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase: Before you start
entries.text:
Gather what isn't plain money in your wallet yet:

- Savings in a vault: withdraw them on the Earn screen.
- Aave V4 supply or a loan: repay and withdraw on the Borrow screen.
- Long or short positions: close them (Close · All) on each position's page.
- The agent wallet: Settings → Agent wallet → Return to my wallet.
- Any other token can go out with Withdraw as itself on Arc, or converted to USDC to cross to another chain.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase: Part 1: with Kawase (the exit kit)
entries.text:
### Pause the agent
Settings → Wallet & limits → Pause all. Everything the agent does without asking stops at once. Your own Face ID
payments still work.

### Revoke every permission
In the exit kit, hold to revoke. One Face ID sends one transaction that revokes every grant on that network: your
allowance and every automation's grant. Automations end. Repeat on the other network if you used it.

### Withdraw everything
In the exit kit, move the money out opens Withdraw with everything
selected (or say "withdraw everything to my Kraken"). Pick where it goes: an exchange (Kraken, Bybit, OKX, Binance,
Bitget, KuCoin, or Coinbase through Base), your own wallet on Arc or another chain, or your bank through an exchange.
Kawase plans each token (a transfer, a bridge, or a conversion to USDC first), warns you about anything the destination
wouldn't credit, and you confirm once with Face ID.

### Check the explorer
Open your address on the explorer (below) and confirm the balances are where you sent them.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase: Part 2: without Kawase (export your wallet)
entries.text:
Your wallet's key is held for you by Privy, split up in secure enclaves. Exporting gives you your own copy of the
private key, so you can use the same account in any wallet.

### Export
Settings → Account → Export wallet. Read the warnings and hold the button: Privy shows your private key in its
own secure window, which Kawase never sees. On a phone the export opens on the web app, where you sign in with the same
email. Keep the key somewhere safe offline. Anyone with it controls your money.

### Import it into another wallet
In MetaMask, Rabby or another wallet that allows custom networks, choose to import a private key. You get the same
address as in Kawase.

### Add Arc
Add the network with the details in the table below. Your balances appear as they are on chain.

### Move your money
Send from that wallet as you would from any other. Vault, Aave and margin positions live in your own account at those
protocols, so any interface for them on Arc can manage them.

Export while Kawase is running if you want a copy you control: the export goes through the app.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase: Check everything on the explorer
entries.text:
You don't need Kawase to see your money. Open your address on Arc's block explorer:

- Mainnet: https://explorer.arc.io/address/<your address>
- Testnet: https://testnet.arcscan.app/address/<your address>

There you can see:

- your balances (on Arc, USDC is also the network's gas token: one balance, shown both as the native coin and as the USDC
  token);
- every transaction, including the payments the agent made under your allowance;
- your account's code: after setup it is 0xef0100 followed by the EIP7702StatelessDeleGator address. That is the
  EIP-7702 upgrade; your account still works as a normal account.

Kawase's receipts link to these same pages.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase: If Kawase disappears
entries.text:
- The agent's permissions stop being useful. Your allowance and automation grants can only be used by Kawase's own agent
  wallet, and they expire: the allowance after 90 days, each automation at its end date.
- Your money stays in your account. It is an ordinary account on Arc.
- With an exported private key (part 2), you can move everything from any wallet that supports Arc.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase: Adding Arc to another wallet
entries.text:
| | Mainnet | Testnet |
|---|---|---|
| Network name | Arc | Arc Testnet |
| Chain ID | 5042 | 5042002 |
| RPC | https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io | https://rpc.testnet.arc.io |
| Currency symbol | USDC | USDC |
| Explorer | https://explorer.arc.io | https://testnet.arcscan.app |

Some wallets label the gas balance "ETH" on custom networks; on Arc it is USDC. The USDC token address is
0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 on both networks; EURC is
0xbEf5f6d51CB62b58e6A8f77868681825C6fe21c1 on mainnet and 0x89B50855Aa3bE2F677cD6303Cec089B5F319D72a on testnet.

entries.title: Withdraw without Kawase: Removing the EIP-7702 upgrade (optional)
entries.text:
You don't need to undo the upgrade to move your money. If you want a plain account again after exporting it, sign an
EIP-7702 authorization pointing at the zero address and send it from the account itself, for example with viem:

Afterwards the explorer shows no code on your address.
